answer: Providers and deployers of AI systems must take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy for their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf [1]. When doing so, they must consider technical knowledge, experience, education, training, the context of use, and the persons or groups affected by the AI systems [1].

Under the AI Act, prohibited AI practices include the placing on the market, putting into service, or use of an AI system that deploys subliminal techniques beyond a person’s consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques [1]. The objective or effect of these techniques must be to materially distort the behaviour of a person or a group of persons by appreciably [1]. Additionally, AI systems used to detect the emotional state of individuals in situations related to the workplace and education are prohibited [2].

According to the EU AI Act, an 'AI system' is defined as a machine-based system that is designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment [2]. It infers, from the input it receives, how to achieve explicit or implicit objectives [2].

answer: An AI system is considered high-risk if it is listed in Annex III [1], [5]. Additionally, an AI system is classified as high-risk if it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product covered by Union harmonization legislation, and fulfills the conditions set out in Article 6 classification rules [2].

The risk-management system for high-risk AI systems should adopt the most appropriate risk-management measures in light of the state of the art in AI, which includes documenting and explaining the choices made and involving experts and external stakeholders when relevant [1]. It must consist of a continuous, iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of the system [2]. This process should aim at identifying and mitigating relevant risks on health, safety, and fundamental rights [2]. Additionally, the system should be regularly reviewed and updated to ensure its continuing effectiveness, along with the justification and documentation of any changes [2].

High-risk AI systems that use techniques involving the training of AI models must be developed on the basis of training, validation, and testing data sets that meet specific quality criteria [1]. These data sets must be subject to data governance [1]. Furthermore, the training, validation, and testing data sets must be relevant, sufficiently representative, free of errors to the best extent possible, and complete in view of the intended purpose [5]. They also need to have appropriate statistical properties, including regarding the persons or groups of persons the system is intended to be used for [5].

High-risk AI systems must technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system [1, 2]. These logging capabilities must enable the recording of events relevant for identifying situations that may result in the system presenting a risk or in a substantial modification, facilitating post-market monitoring, and monitoring the operation of high-risk AI systems [5]. Specifically for systems referred to in point 1(a) of Annex III, the logging capabilities must at a minimum record the period of each use of the system, including the start date and time and end date and time [5].

answer: High-risk AI systems must be designed and developed so that natural persons can effectively oversee them while in use, aiming to prevent or minimize risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights [1]. Appropriate human oversight measures should be identified by the provider before the system is placed on the market or put into service [4]. Such oversight enables assigned natural persons to understand the system's capacities and limitations, monitor its operation to detect anomalies, and remain aware of the risk of over-relying on its output [2]. Additionally, high-risk systems should include mechanisms to guide and inform these individuals to make informed intervention decisions or stop the system if it malfunctions [3].

Deployers of high-risk AI systems must take appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure they use the systems in accordance with the accompanying instructions for use [2]. They play a critical role in protecting fundamental rights, complementing the provider's obligations, by identifying potential significant risks based on their precise knowledge of the concrete context of use [1].
The deployer of the high-risk AI system must carry out the fundamental rights impact assessment [1, 2].

Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake must disclose that the content has been artificially created or manipulated by labelling the output accordingly and disclosing its artificial origin [1, 2]. For certain works, this transparency obligation is limited to disclosing the existence of such generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display, enjoyment, or normal exploitation of the work, while maintaining its utility and quality [3].

answer: Providers of general-purpose AI models must draw up and keep up-to-date technical documentation [2]. In the case of a modification or fine-tuning of a model, their obligations should be limited to that specific modification or fine-tuning [3]. Additionally, providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk must perform model evaluation using standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing [4]. They must also assess and mitigate possible risks [4].

In the event of a person's death, the report must be provided not later than 10 days after the provider or deployer becomes aware of the serious incident [1]. Otherwise, the report must be made not later than 15 days after the provider or, where applicable, the deployer becomes aware of the serious incident [2].

Yes, a person affected by certain AI systems that produce legal effects or similarly significantly affect them in a way they consider to have an adverse impact on their health, safety, or fundamental rights has the right to obtain clear and meaningful explanations from the deployer regarding the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken [2].
Non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices referred to in Article 5 shall be subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 1 500 000 [1].

The Commission may impose fines on providers of general-purpose AI models not exceeding 3% of their annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher [1]. This applies when the Commission finds that the provider has intentionally or negligently infringed the relevant provisions of the regulation or failed to comply with a document or information request [1].

In order for processing to be lawful, personal data should be processed on the basis of the consent of the data subject concerned or some other legitimate basis laid down by law, either in the GDPR or in other Union or Member State law [3]. Additionally, the legal basis provided by Union or Member State law for the processing of personal data may also provide a legal basis for further processing [4].

Yes, the data subject has the right to withdraw their consent at any time [1]. The withdrawal of consent must be as easy to withdraw as it is to give it [4]. Furthermore, the request for consent must be presented in a manner that is clearly distinguishable from other matters, intelligible, easily accessible, and written in clear and plain language [1]. Prior to giving consent, the data subject must be informed of their right to withdraw it [4]. When assessing if consent is freely given, utmost account must be taken of whether the performance of a contract or service is conditional on consent to process personal data that is not necessary for that performance [4].

Under the GDPR, the processing of a child's personal data in relation to information society services is lawful where the child is at least 16 years old [1]. However, Member States may provide by law for a lower age, provided that it is not below 13 years [4].

Under the right of access, the data subject has the right to obtain confirmation as to whether or not personal data concerning them are being processed, and where that is the case, access to the personal data [1]. Additionally, they receive information on the purposes of the processing, the categories of personal data concerned, and the recipients or categories of recipients to whom the data have been or will be disclosed [1].

A data subject has the right to erasure ('right to be forgotten') when the retention of the personal data infringes the GDPR or Union or Member State law to which the controller is subject [1]. Furthermore, this right applies when personal data are no longer necessary for the purposes for which they were collected or otherwise processed, or when the data subject has withdrawn consent or objects to the processing [1, 2].

The right to data portability allows a data subject to receive the personal data concerning them, which they have provided to a controller, in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format [3, 4]. It also includes the right to have the personal data transmitted directly from one controller to another, where technically feasible, if the processing is carried out by automated means [4]. This right applies when the data was provided based on consent or for the performance of a contract, but it does not apply to processing necessary for the performance of a public task [1, 4].

A data subject has the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning them or similarly significantly affects them [1, 2]. Furthermore, they have the right to obtain meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such automated decision-making [4].

A personal data breach must be notified to the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after the controller has become aware of it [1, 3]. This requirement applies unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons [1, 3]. If the notification is not made within 72 hours, it must be accompanied by reasons for the delay [2].

A data protection impact assessment is required prior to processing in cases likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, taking into account the nature, scope, context, and purposes of the processing [3]. Specifically, it is required for a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing, including profiling, that produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects natural persons [4]. It is also required for the processing on a large scale of special categories of data, biometric data, or data relating to criminal convictions and offences, as well as for the large-scale monitoring of publicly accessible areas using optic-electronic devices [1, 2, 4]. Furthermore, it is required for operations where the supervisory authority considers the processing likely to result in a high risk, particularly when it prevents data subjects from exercising a right, using a service, or performing a contract [1].

The controller and processor must designate a data protection officer in any case where the processing is carried out by a public authority or body (except for courts acting in their judicial capacity) [4]. Additionally, a data protection officer must be designated if the core activities of the controller or processor consist of processing operations requiring regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale [4]. Furthermore, state law may also designate a data protection officer [1].

Under the GDPR, certain infringements are subject to administrative fines of up to 20 000 000 EUR, or up to 4 % of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [4]. Additionally, infringements of other specified provisions are subject to administrative fines of up to 10 000 000 EUR, or up to 2 % of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [5].

Bei geschlossenen Systemen erfolgt die Datenverarbeitung in einer eingegrenzten, technisch abgeschlossenen Umgebung mit nur einem eng begrenzten Anwenderkreis, während die Kontrolle über die Ein- und Ausgabedaten bei den Anwendenden liegt [1]. Offene Systeme werden hingegen beispielsweise als Cloud-Lösung vom Anbietenden betrieben und sind über das Internet für einen unbestimmten Anwenderkreis zugänglich [2]. Zudem verlassen bei offenen Systemen die Eingabedaten den geschützten Bereich der Anwendenden und können je nach Konzeption auch für die Beantwortung von Anfragen anderer Anwender genutzt werden [2].

Vor dem Einsatz einer KI-Anwendung ist eine Datenschutz-Folgenabschätzung (DSFA) nach Art. 35 DS-GVO erforderlich, wenn die Vorabprüfung ergibt, dass die Verarbeitung voraussichtlich ein hohes Risiko für die Rechte und Freiheiten natürlicher Personen zur Folge hat [1, 2]. Beim Einsatz von KI-Anwendungen wird dies vielfach der Fall sein [2]. Darüber hinaus veröffentlichen die Datenschutzaufsichtsbehörden sogenannte „Muss-Listen“ zu Verarbeitungen, für die eine DSFA durchgeführt werden muss [2].
Beschäftigte sollten keine privaten Accounts und Geräte für KI-Anwendungen nutzen, da auf diese Weise Profile zu den jeweiligen Beschäftigten entstehen können [1, 2].

Zudem haben betroffene Personen bei Unrichtigkeit personenbezogener Daten ein Recht auf Berichtigung, das in der KI-Anwendung umsetzbar sein muss [2].
